summary: The talk opens with the polarized discourse on AI coding agents, citing Jonathan Blow, Jesse Friselle, Eric S. Raymond, and Thomas Tachek. Liu references Jeff Huntley's observations that developers were 'holding it wrong'—using new agents with old mental models. He frames three eras: GPT-3 autocomplete (2022), ChatGPT chatbots/ragbots (2023), and the current agent era requiring autonomous file editing and command execution. Controversial design decisions include: agents should edit directly without per-turn confirmation; thick VS Code forks may be obsolete; agentic chains deeply couple to specific LLMs making model swapping impractical; fixed pricing incentivizes dumb models; Unix philosophy beats vertical integration; and Sourcegraph built Amp from scratch rather than extending Cody. Amp ships as two deliberately bare-bones clients—a VS Code extension and CLI—both centered on a text box. Liu demos Amp on its own codebase, implementing a Linear connector icon customization. Amp autonomously searches Linear via MCP, spins off sub-agents, reads Svelte frontend files, plans with a to-do list, makes incremental edits, and runs tests. The demo reveals multi-threaded workflows and the VS Code diff view as primary review surface. The agent discovers an existing mechanism for plumbing non-secret config to the UI, correctly whitelisting only the endpoint URL. Liu then details power user best practices: writing long detailed prompts (Amp defaults enter to newline, requiring command+enter to submit), constructing front-end feedback loops via Playwright MCP and Storybook for fast iteration, directing agents to relevant context when working with out-of-distribution codebases, using agents for code understanding and onboarding (citing new hire Tyler Bruno), leveraging agents for thorough code reviews by consuming large diffs and generating summaries, and using sub-agents to preserve context window quality (noting Sonnet 4 degrades around 120-130K of its 200K window). Anti-patterns include micromanaging, under-prompting, and using agents to TLDR code. The top 1% run multiple agents in parallel—Jeff Huntley constructs prompts for 3-4 agents on different compiler parts, hits enter, and sleeps. Liu frames agent wielding as a high-ceiling skill comparable to mastering an editor or programming language, with thread sharing built into Amp for knowledge dissemination. He closes by offering $10 in free credits for trying Amp, and in a brief Q&A acknowledges his habit of correcting typos during live demos—partly paranoia from 2023-era models—while noting modern LLMs are increasingly typo-robust.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & The State of AI in Coding
sections.summary: Liu surveys the polarized debate around AI coding agents, citing viewpoints from Jonathan Blow, Jesse Friselle, Eric S. Raymond, and a Hacker News post by Thomas Tachek, and references Jeff Huntley's observations of developers 'holding it wrong.' The number one mistake is using new agents with old mental models from six months ago, driven by a step function transition in model capabilities.

sections.title: The Three Eras of AI Coding Tools
sections.summary: Liu frames the evolution from GPT-3 text-completion copilots/autocomplete (2022) to ChatGPT-era instruct-tuned chatbots and ragbots combining chat with retrieval (2023) to the current agent era requiring a new application architecture where the LLM can edit files, run commands, and operate autonomously.

sections.title: Controversial Design Philosophy for Agents
sections.summary: Liu presents spicy design takes: agents should edit autonomously; thick VS Code forks may be obsolete; model swapping is impractical in agentic chains; fixed pricing incentivizes dumb models; Unix philosophy beats vertical integration; Sourcegraph built 'Amp' from scratch rather than extending 'Cody.'

sections.title: Internet Portal Analogy & Amp UI Design
sections.summary: Liu compares early internet portal directories to a single search box, foreshadowing agent UI simplification. Amp ships as two deliberately bare-bones clients—a VS Code extension leveraging diff views and a composable CLI—both centered on a simple text box, reflecting the Unix philosophy.

sections.title: Live Demo: Customizing the Linear Connector Icon
sections.summary: Liu demos Amp on its own codebase, asking it to find and implement a real Linear issue about customizing the Linear connector icon. Amp autonomously calls the Linear API via MCP, spins off sub-agents for agentic search, reads Svelte frontend files, plans with a to-do list, makes incremental edits, and runs tests. Liu highlights multi-threaded workflows and the VS Code diff view as primary review surface.

sections.title: Emergent Power User Patterns
sections.summary: Liu introduces emergent patterns from Amp's curated power user community. Average agent spend exceeds chatbot/autocomplete spend, with huge variance—top users spend thousands monthly on inference. Power users write very long detailed prompts, informing Amp's product design.

sections.title: Best Practices: Detailed Prompts & Feedback Loops
sections.summary: Power users write long detailed prompts because LLMs are programmable with context. Amp defaults the enter key to newline, requiring command+enter to submit, pushing users toward longer prompts. A dominant paradigm is constructing front-end feedback loops via Playwright MCP and Storybook, letting agents snapshot UI changes and loop back quickly. When agents hit out-of-distribution code, power users direct them to relevant context like build commands and test invocations. The demo completes successfully—Amp discovers an existing mechanism for plumbing non-secret config to the UI, correctly whitelisting only the endpoint URL.

sections.title: Code Understanding & Code Reviews
sections.summary: Contrary to the narrative that agents make programmers lazy, power users use agents to better understand code. New hire Tyler Bruno uses Amp to ramp up on how different pieces connect and draw diagrams. Users also leverage agents for thorough code reviews—consuming large diffs, generating high-level summaries, and identifying entry points, lowering the activation energy that often causes people to postpone reviews.

sections.title: Sub-Agents, Anti-Patterns & Parallel Agents
sections.summary: Sub-agents preserve context window quality—LLMs degrade around 120-130K tokens despite 200K nominal windows (e.g., Sonnet 4). Anti-patterns include micromanaging, under-prompting, and using agents to TLDR code rather than reviewing thoroughly. The top 1% run multiple agents in parallel—Jeff Huntley constructs prompts for 3-4 agents on different compiler parts, hits enter, and sleeps. Liu frames agent wielding as a high-ceiling skill comparable to mastering an editor or language, with Amp's thread sharing mechanism enabling knowledge dissemination across teams.

sections.title: Closing Remarks & Q&A
sections.summary: Liu closes by offering $10 in free credits for attendees interested in trying Amp. In a brief Q&A, an audience member notes Liu still corrects typos during the demo despite advising against it. Liu acknowledges it is partly habit and partly paranoia from 2023-era models that could go off the rails from typo tokens, but notes modern LLMs are increasingly typo-robust.
